---
title: "Gaussian random slopes, penalized least squares and REML"
jupyter: python3
---

The [random-intercept walkthrough](lmm-math.qmd) introduces clustering. Here we
allow each subject both a different starting reaction time and a different
response to days of sleep deprivation, using the published sleepstudy data. The [optimizer audit](r-compatibility.qmd) verifies
this model against R lme4 and statsmodels under ML and REML.

## Observations and matrices

$$
y_i=o_i+x_i^\top\beta+z_i^\top b_{g(i)}+\epsilon_i,
\qquad b_g\sim N(0,\Sigma),\quad
\epsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2/w_i).
$$

Here o is a known offset, w is a positive prior weight, x contains fixed predictors
and z contains random predictors. For sleepstudy, o=0, w=1 and both local designs
have `[1, Days]` columns. The ones construct an intercept; Days is observed data.
Beta contains the population intercept and slope. Each group's b contains deviations
from those population coefficients, not a second set of observed predictors.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display,Math
ROOT=next(p for p in [Path.cwd(),*Path.cwd().parents] if (p/'Cargo.toml').exists())
fixtures=json.loads((ROOT/'tests/fixtures/lmm-expanded-r.json').read_text())
c=next(c for c in fixtures['cases'] if c['name']=='sleepstudy_reml')
x=np.array(c['x']);y=np.array(c['y']);z=np.array(c['terms'][0]['z']);groups=np.array(c['terms'][0]['groups'])
raw=pd.read_csv(ROOT/'docs/data/lmm/sleepstudy.csv')
display(raw.head(8))
print('X:',x.shape,'y:',y.shape,'local random design:',z.shape)
def matrix_tex(a,name):
    a=np.atleast_2d(a)
    body=r' \\ '.join(' & '.join(f'{v:.5g}' for v in row) for row in a)
    display(Math(name+r'=\begin{bmatrix}'+body+r'\end{bmatrix}'))
# Show observed inputs, not guesses at beta.
matrix_tex(x[:4],'X_{\mathrm{first\ four}}')
matrix_tex(y[:4,None],'y_{\mathrm{first\ four}}')
```

The global Z has separate columns for each subject. Four rows for each of the
first two groups illustrate its block pattern:

```{python}
order=list(dict.fromkeys(groups));g_index={g:i for i,g in enumerate(order)}
Z=np.zeros((len(y),2*len(order)))
for i,g in enumerate(groups):Z[i,2*g_index[g]:2*g_index[g]+2]=z[i]
ids=np.r_[np.flatnonzero(groups==order[0])[:4],np.flatnonzero(groups==order[1])[:4]]
matrix_tex(Z[np.ix_(ids,range(4))],'Z_{\mathrm{excerpt}}')
print('Full Z:',Z.shape,'= observations × all random coefficients')
```

A zero means that another subject's random coefficients do not contribute to this
observation. Crossed models add more independent blocks, for example subject and
site. Nested models supply distinct parent/child identifiers. Independent slopes
constrain the corresponding covariance to a diagonal matrix.

## Covariance through a Cholesky factor

Instead of optimizing variance/correlation entries directly, optimize a lower
triangular relative factor:

$$
L=\begin{bmatrix}a&0\\c&d\end{bmatrix},\qquad a,d\geq0,
\qquad\Sigma=\sigma^2LL^\top
=\sigma^2\begin{bmatrix}a^2&ac\\ac&c^2+d^2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This guarantees positive semidefinite covariance, including valid zero-variance
or perfect-correlation boundaries. A negative c can represent negative
intercept/slope covariance. lme4's lower-triangle parameter ordering is column-major:
`[a, c, d]`. Several terms concatenate their parameters in supplied term order.

```{python}
from scipy.linalg import cholesky
reference=c['references']['bobyqa']['result']
Sigma=np.array(reference['terms'][0]['covariance'])
sigma2=reference['residual_variance'];L=cholesky(Sigma/sigma2,lower=True)
matrix_tex(L,'L');matrix_tex(sigma2*L@L.T,r'\widehat\Sigma')
print('Intercept SD (ms):',np.sqrt(Sigma[0,0]))
print('Slope SD (ms/day):',np.sqrt(Sigma[1,1]))
print('Intercept/slope correlation:',Sigma[0,1]/np.sqrt(Sigma[0,0]*Sigma[1,1]))
```

These are estimates from the full sample.
The off-diagonal dot product `a*c + 0*d` produces the covariance after multiplying
by sigma². Variances have different physical units because the second coefficient
is measured in milliseconds per day.

## Penalized least squares profiles out beta and random effects

Repeat L once per group to construct block-diagonal Lambda. Write b=Lambda u,
where u has spherical covariance sigma²I. Given theta, minimize

$$
q(\theta)=\min_{u,\beta}
\left\|W^{1/2}(y-o-X\beta-Z\Lambda u)\right\|^2+\|u\|^2.
$$

The first term fits observed reaction times; the second penalizes implausibly
large standardized random effects. This is a consequence of their Gaussian
likelihood, not an arbitrary regularization parameter chosen by the user.
It is the least-squares problem

$$
\begin{bmatrix}W^{1/2}Z\Lambda&W^{1/2}X\\I&0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}u\\\beta\end{bmatrix}
\approx\begin{bmatrix}W^{1/2}(y-o)\\0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For a selected theta, linear algebra finds u and beta. The nonlinear optimizer
searches theta only. We solve with QR; coefficients do not come from explicitly
inverting a normal-equation matrix.

```{python}
from scipy.linalg import block_diag,solve_triangular
Lambda=block_diag(*([L]*len(order)))
A=np.block([[Z@Lambda,x],[np.eye(Z.shape[1]),np.zeros((Z.shape[1],x.shape[1]))]])
b=np.r_[y,np.zeros(Z.shape[1])]
Q,R=np.linalg.qr(A,mode='reduced');solution=solve_triangular(R,Q.T@b)
u=solution[:Z.shape[1]];beta=solution[Z.shape[1]:];effects=Lambda@u
residual=y-x@beta-Z@effects
q=residual@residual+u@u
print('Augmented design:',A.shape)
print('beta:',beta)
print('Observation residual contribution:',residual@residual)
print('Random-effect penalty contribution:',u@u)
print('Total profiled q:',q)
assert np.allclose(beta,reference['coefficients'],rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-8)
assert np.allclose(effects.reshape(-1,2),reference['terms'][0]['effects'],rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-8)
```

The code uses an additional QR compression before optimization. QR of weighted
`[Z, X/scales, y-offset]` preserves every trial residual norm. Each trial needs
only that compact square-root summary plus identity penalty rows. This extends
the earlier cached random-intercept idea. The current general summary is dense;
lme4 uses sparse factorization to support larger random designs.

## ML and REML are different objectives

With C=W⁻¹+Z Lambda Lambdaᵀ Zᵀ, the profiled Gaussian ML scale is

$$\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=q/n.$$

The negative profiled marginal log-likelihood is

$$
-\ell_{ML}(\theta)=\tfrac12\left[
 n\{\log(2\pi)+1+\log(q/n)\}+\log|C|
\right].
$$

REML adjusts for estimating the p fixed coefficients. It uses

$$
\hat\sigma^2_{REML}=q/(n-p),
$$

and the restricted criterion

$$
-\ell_{REML}(\theta)=\tfrac12\left[
(n-p)\{\log(2\pi)+1+\log(q/(n-p))\}
+\log|C|+\log|X^\top C^{-1}X|
\right].
$$

REML changes the optimization objective, not merely the final denominator.
Its extra determinant accounts for fixed-effect estimation. Both determinants
come from triangular QR factors in our implementation. Scaling fixed columns
requires restoring their determinant contribution, even though scaling does not
change the fitted mean. REML likelihood values should not compare different
fixed-effect designs.

```{python}
qr_random=R[:Z.shape[1],:Z.shape[1]]
qr_fixed=R[Z.shape[1]:,Z.shape[1]:]
logdet_C=2*np.log(abs(np.diag(qr_random))).sum()
logdet_info=2*np.log(abs(np.diag(qr_fixed))).sum()
df=len(y)-x.shape[1]
reml_variance=q/df
reml_ll=-.5*(df*(np.log(2*np.pi)+1+np.log(reml_variance))+logdet_C+logdet_info)
print('n, p, n-p:',len(y),x.shape[1],df)
print('q/(n-p):',reml_variance)
print('log determinant C:',logdet_C)
print('log determinant fixed information:',logdet_info)
print('Restricted log-likelihood:',reml_ll)
assert np.isclose(reml_ll,reference['log_likelihood'],rtol=0,atol=1e-8)
```

## Fixed-effect uncertainty

At the fitted variance components, the plug-in covariance is

$$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)=\hat\sigma^2(X^\top C^{-1}X)^{-1}.$$

The fixed triangular QR block supplies this through triangular solves.
Standard errors are square roots of its diagonal. Our mixed-model z tests and
95% intervals are normal Wald approximations; this does not supply finite-group
Student t degrees of freedom or variance-component confidence intervals.

```{python}
R_inv=solve_triangular(qr_fixed,np.eye(x.shape[1]))
cov_beta=reml_variance*R_inv@R_inv.T
matrix_tex(cov_beta,r'\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)')
print('Standard errors:',np.sqrt(cov_beta.diagonal()))
assert np.allclose(cov_beta,reference['covariance'],rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-8)
```

The implementation is `crates/stats-core/src/lmm.rs`. Owned Vec inputs become
nalgebra matrices; term/result structs preserve the array shapes and term order.
`Result` propagates invalid designs, failed controls and nonconvergence to the
PHP binding as exceptions. The binding validates and filters all aligned inputs,
then returns plain arrays.


## Four grouping levels: which observations share variation?

The same construction handles multiple nested terms. For repeated assessments
within students, classes, schools and districts,

$$
y_i=x_i^\top\beta+d_{D(i)}+s_{S(i)}+c_{C(i)}+t_{T(i)}+\epsilon_i.
$$

Each term has its own Gaussian variance and is independent of the other terms.
Conditional on the fixed design, two different observations share covariance
only through common groups:

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(y_i,y_j\mid X)
=\tau_D^2\mathbf{1}_{D(i)=D(j)}
+\tau_S^2\mathbf{1}_{S(i)=S(j)}
+\tau_C^2\mathbf{1}_{C(i)=C(j)}
+\tau_T^2\mathbf{1}_{T(i)=T(j)},\quad i\ne j.
$$

On the diagonal, add the observation variance sigma² (or sigma²/w_i with weights).
The grouping IDs must be globally unique within each term: a local school number
needs its district in the key, and a local student number needs all its parents.
Three grouping terms plus observations are often called a four-level model; here
we name the number of grouping terms explicitly.

```{python}
# Demonstrate the covariance implied by the fitted four-grouping-level model.
# This small matrix is for teaching; the native engine never constructs full V.
report=json.loads((ROOT/'docs/verifications/r-compatibility-results.json').read_text())
case=next(r for r in report['mixed'] if r['name']=='nested_4_grouping_levels_reml')
fit=case['PHP']['bobyqa']
input_case=next(r for r in fixtures['cases'] if r['name']==case['name'])
variances=np.array([t['covariance'][0][0] for t in fit['random']])
# First pair: same student; then different student, class, school and district.
selected=[0,1,4,8,16,32]
V=np.eye(len(selected))*fit['residual_variance']
for term,var in zip(input_case['terms'],variances):
    ids=np.array(term['groups'])[selected]
    V+=var*(ids[:,None]==ids[None,:])
display(pd.DataFrame(dict(grouping=['district','school','class','student'],
                          groups=[len(t['group_labels']) for t in fit['random']],
                          variance=variances)))
matrix_tex(V,r'V_{\mathrm{six\ observations}}')
print('Same student:',V[0,1])
print('Same class, different students:',V[0,2])
print('Same school, different classes:',V[0,3])
print('Same district, different schools:',V[0,4])
print('Different districts:',V[0,5])
assert np.isclose(V[0,1],variances.sum())
assert np.isclose(V[0,2],variances[:3].sum())
assert np.isclose(V[0,3],variances[:2].sum())
assert np.isclose(V[0,4],variances[0])
assert V[0,5]==0
```

The [expanded audit](r-compatibility.qmd#more-than-two-grouping-levels) checks all
observations and effects in three- and four-grouping-level cases, under ML and
REML, with both native optimizers and all four actual lme4 wrappers. There is no
two-level restriction in the API; the current dense size limits still apply.
